chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, from Abdullah ibn Sinan who said:

I attended the Maghrib prayer on a rainy night in the mosque of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family). When it was close to the twilight, they called the adhan and established the iqama, and they prayed Maghrib. Then they gave the people time until they had prayed two rak'at. Then the muadhdhin stood up in his place in the mosque, and he established the prayer, and they prayed Isha. Then the people dispersed to their homes.
So I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about that, and he said: Yes, indeed the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) used to do this.

key_terms.أمهلوا: They gave respite/waited — indicating a brief interval between the two combined prayers
key_terms.الجمع: Combining (jam') — the practice of combining two prayers, here Maghrib with Isha
key_terms.الشفق: The twilight (afterglow) — in Shia jurisprudence, this marks the end of the Maghrib prayer time

ai.seo_question: Did the Prophet combine Maghrib and Isha prayer on rainy nights?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) records a firsthand witness account by Abdullah ibn Sinan of the combining (jam') of Maghrib and Isha prayers at the Prophet's mosque on a rainy night, with the Imam confirming this was the Prophet's own practice. The narration establishes a jurisprudential precedent (sunnah) for combining the two evening prayers due to rain. In early Islamic practice, the community would gather in the Prophet's mosque, and accommodation of weather conditions was a recognized basis for combining prayers, reflecting the religion's emphasis on easing hardship for the community.
